Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Area equals 11 times 7, which is 77 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 16 into 10 and 6. Multiply 25 by 10. 25 times 10 equals 250.
Now multiply 25 by 6. 25 times 6 equals 150.
Add the two parts. So the area is 400 square centimetres. 250 plus 150 equals 400.

Q_CH20_017.q: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are:
hints: Think about what a parallelogram looks like: a rectangle that has been pushed over to one side. Look at each pair of sides that face each other.
The name of the shape gives a clue about one property of its opposite sides. Then think about whether the two sides facing each other are the same length.

Similar example: in a trapezium, one pair of opposite sides is parallel, but those two sides are not the same length, and the other pair is not parallel at all. Ask the same two questions about a parallelogram: are the opposite sides parallel, and are they equal? Drawing one will help.
steps: The word parallelogram comes from the word parallel. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, which means they run in the same direction and never meet.
Measure the sides of any parallelogram and you find that each side is the same length as the side facing it.
So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal.

Q_CH20_018.q: In a rhombus, the axes of symmetry are:
options: There are no axes of symmetry
hints: A rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry. What are they?
If you fold a rhombus along either diagonal, both halves match perfectly.
The diagonals are the axes of symmetry.
steps: A rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry.
These axes are its two diagonals.

Q_CH20_019.q: Which of the following statements is true?
hints: Each statement says that every shape of one kind is also a shape of another kind. To test one, ask whether the first shape always has everything the second shape needs.

Write down what each shape needs. A rectangle needs four right angles. A square needs four right angles and four equal sides. A rhombus needs four equal sides. A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides.

Similar example: is every square a rhombus? A rhombus needs four equal sides. Every square has four equal sides, so every square is a rhombus. Test each statement in the same way, by checking what the second shape needs.
steps: A rectangle is a four-sided shape with four right angles. A square has four right angles and also four equal sides.
Every square has four right angles, so every square has all that a rectangle needs.

The other statements can each be shown untrue with one drawing: a slanted rhombus has no right angles, a slanted parallelogram has no right angles, and a long rectangle does not have four equal sides.
The true statement is: Every square is a rectangle.

Q_CH20_019_V09.q: A rectangle is 26 centimetres long and 24 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 26 times 24 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 12 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. Area equals 12 times 5, which is 60 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 24 into 20 and 4. Multiply 26 by 20. 26 times 20 equals 520.
Now multiply 26 by 4. 26 times 4 equals 104.
Add the two parts. So the area is 624 square centimetres. 520 plus 104 equals 624.

Q_CH20_020.q: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a:
hints: Different quadrilaterals have different numbers of pairs of parallel sides. Go through the shapes you know and count the parallel pairs in each.
A parallelogram and a rhombus each have two pairs of parallel sides. Look for the shape that has just one pair.

Similar example: which quadrilateral has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, but not always four equal sides? Checking the shapes one by one, the rectangle fits. Check the shapes for parallel pairs in the same way.
steps: Count the pairs of parallel sides in each shape. A parallelogram has two pairs, and a rhombus also has two pairs.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, but usually no parallel sides at all.
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides, and its other two sides are not parallel.
So a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is called a trapezium.

Q_CH20_021.q: A kite has how many axes of symmetry?
hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly. Picture a kite, with two shorter sides at the top and two longer sides at the bottom.
Try folding the kite along each of its two corner-to-corner lines. Count only the folds where one half lands exactly on the other.

Similar example: a rhombus has four equal sides. Folding it along either of its corner-to-corner lines makes the halves match, so a rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry. The sides of a kite are not all equal, so test each of its folds with care.
steps: A kite has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other: two shorter sides and two longer sides.
Fold along the line that joins the corner where the short sides meet to the corner where the long sides meet. One half lands exactly on the other, so this is an axis of symmetry.
Fold along the other corner-to-corner line. A short side would land on a long side, so the halves do not match.
A kite has 1 axis of symmetry.

Q_CH20_022.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90 degrees, 85 degrees, and 110 degrees. What is the fourth angle?
hints: The four angles of any quadrilateral always add up to the same total. If you know three of them, the fourth is what is left.
The four angles add up to 360 degrees. Start by adding the three angles you know: 90 degrees, 85 degrees and 110 degrees.
Similar example: three angles of a quadrilateral are 80 degrees, 100 degrees and 120 degrees. They add to 300 degrees. The fourth angle is 360 degrees minus 300 degrees, which is 60 degrees.
steps: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
Add the three angles you know. 90 degrees plus 85 degrees plus 110 degrees, which is 285 degrees.
Take that from 360 degrees to find the fourth angle. 360 degrees minus 285 degrees, which is 75 degrees.
The fourth angle is 75 degrees.

Q_CH20_023.q: The area of a square is 144 square centimetres. What is its side?
hints: The area of a square is its side multiplied by itself. Here you work backwards from the area to the side.
Look for a number that gives 144 when it is multiplied by itself. Try numbers a little bigger than 10, since 10 times 10 equals 100.

Similar example: a square has an area of 169 square centimetres. 10 times 10 equals 100, which is too small and 15 times 15 equals 225, which is too big. Trying 13 gives 13 times 13, which is 169, so the side is 13 centimetres.
steps: The area of a square is side times side, so find a number that multiplied by itself gives 144.
10 times 10 equals 100, which is too small, and 11 times 11 equals 121, which is still too small.
The next number to try is 12, and it gives exactly the area. 12 times 12 equals 144.
The side of the square is 12 centimetres.

Q_CH20_023_V04.q: A rectangle is 23 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. What is its area?
hints: This asks for area, the space inside the rectangle. Think about how the length and the width work together to cover it.
The area of a rectangle is length times width. Set up 23 times 7 and work it out.
Here is a similar one: a rectangle 11 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Area equals 11 times 7, which is 77 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
Split 23 into 20 and 3. Multiply the 20 by 7. 7 times 20 equals 140.
Now multiply the 3 by 7. 7 times 3 equals 21.
Add the two parts. So the area is 161 square centimetres. 140 plus 21 equals 161.

Q_CH20_024.q: A rectangle has area 96 square centimetres and length 12 centimetres. What is its breadth?
hints: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. Here the area and the length are known, so you work backwards with the opposite operation.
Ask yourself: 12 times what number gives 96? You can find it by dividing the area by the length.
Similar example: a rectangle has an area of 70 square centimetres and a length of 14 centimetres. The breadth is 70 divided by 14, which is 5 centimetres, because 14 times 5 equals 70.
steps: Length times breadth gives the area, so 12 times the breadth is 96.
Divide the area by the length. 96 divided by 12 equals 8.
Check: 12 times 8 equals 96. The breadth is 8 centimetres.

Are equal and bisect each other at right angles
Are unequal and do not bisect each other
Are equal but do not bisect at right angles
hints: A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus. Rectangle diagonals are equal. Rhombus diagonals bisect at 90 degrees.
So square diagonals are both equal and bisect at right angles.
